coverage_depth.justification: This is a vendor-delivered patch fix targeting a specific reconnection defect, which limits the functional scope. However, the 6 device/POS version combinations multiply test execution effort significantly, and payment processing carries high financial and data integrity risk. The reconnection logic change could have non-obvious side effects on transaction state management and acquirer integration, warranting thorough integration and exploratory coverage beyond a minimal patch scope.

effort_estimate.notes: Core test cases number approximately 25-30 unique scenarios, but most must be executed across all 6 device/POS combinations (POS v18 + v19 x Terminal A, B, C), multiplying execution runs. Smoke and regression cases may be sampled across combinations rather than exhaustively repeated if device behaviour is confirmed identical. Estimate assumes a small team of 1-2 manual testers with access to all hardware. Integration tests may require coordination with payment processor sandbox environment and could add scheduling overhead not reflected in case count.

coverage_depth.justification: Although this is a targeted bug fix, it involves configuration file changes that carry regression risk across multiple payment types and terminal message states. The specific validation requirement (cloud processing disabled) adds an environmental complexity. Incorrect messaging at the POS directly impacts crew operations and customer experience, and the root cause (mismatched config files or overrides) could have broader unintended side effects on other terminal messages or transaction flows.

effort_estimate.notes: Lower bound assumes a single terminal model, single gift card type, and straightforward config deployment. Upper bound accounts for multiple terminal units, multiple gift card types, testing both cloud-on and cloud-off states, and extended exploratory sessions. A small QA team of 2-3 should be able to complete this within 1-2 test cycles.

exploratory_tests: Rapidly cancel multiple consecutive gift card transactions with cloud processing disabled and observe whether the correct message consistently appears or whether any race condition causes the wrong message to flash or persist.
Attempt to cancel a gift card transaction at the exact moment the terminal is transitioning between states (e.g., during network timeout or reconnect attempt) and observe what message is displayed.
Deliberately introduce a corrupted or missing configuration file and observe how the terminal handles the error — does it fail gracefully or display an unintended message?
Test the cancel flow on a POS terminal that has been running for an extended period (session longevity) to check whether any in-memory configuration drift causes the wrong message to reappear.
Verify behavior when a crew member cancels a gift card transaction immediately after a previous cancellation without returning to idle — check for stale message display.
Check whether the fix holds after a POS terminal software restart or configuration reload, ensuring the corrected files are not overwritten by a default or backup configuration.

Explore whether the message displayed differs based on who initiates the cancel (crew member vs. manager override) and confirm 'CANCEL TRANSACTION' is shown in all applicable crew-initiated cancel scenarios.
functional_tests: With backend cloud processing disabled, initiate a gift card transaction on the POS terminal and cancel it mid-transaction; verify the terminal displays exactly 'CANCEL TRANSACTION' and not 'VOID NEW ITEMS AND CANCEL TRANSACTION'.

With backend cloud processing disabled, cancel a gift card transaction at different stages (e.g., immediately after card swipe, after amount entry, after partial authorization attempt) and confirm 'CANCEL TRANSACTION' is displayed at each stage.
Confirm that after the corrected cancel message displays, the gift card transaction is fully voided/cancelled in the system and no partial charge or authorization remains.
Verify that the corrected configuration files are applied system-wide and no residual override causes 'VOID NEW ITEMS AND CANCEL TRANSACTION' to appear for gift card cancel actions.
Confirm that the cancel message displayed on the POS terminal matches exactly the expected string 'CANCEL TRANSACTION' with correct casing, spacing, and punctuation as defined in the specification.

With backend cloud processing disabled, perform a gift card transaction cancel using different gift card types (e.g., stored-value, promotional) if applicable, and verify the correct message displays for each.
integration_tests: With backend cloud processing disabled, cancel a gift card transaction and verify the backend transaction log or audit trail records the cancellation correctly, independent of the display message shown.

Confirm that the configuration file correction does not cause a mismatch between the terminal display state and the backend transaction state (i.e., terminal shows cancel but backend still holds an open authorization).
Verify that the POS terminal correctly reads and applies the corrected configuration files on startup or reload, and that no cached or overridden configuration from a previous deployment persists.

If the POS terminal communicates cancellation status to a central management or reporting system, verify that the cancellation event is correctly transmitted and recorded when cloud processing is off.
regression_tests: With backend cloud processing enabled (normal operating mode), cancel a gift card transaction and verify the terminal displays the correct message for that configuration state — confirm the fix did not break cloud-on behavior.

Process a successful (non-cancelled) gift card transaction end-to-end with cloud processing disabled and verify it completes normally, confirming the configuration change did not disrupt successful transaction flow.

Cancel a non-gift-card transaction (e.g., credit card, cash) with cloud processing disabled and verify the terminal displays the appropriate cancel message for that payment type — confirming no cross-payment-type message regression.

Verify that 'VOID NEW ITEMS AND CANCEL TRANSACTION' still appears correctly in any legitimate workflow where it is the expected message (e.g., voiding new items on a non-gift-card transaction), confirming the fix is scoped only to gift card cancel.

Perform a gift card transaction cancel with cloud processing disabled across multiple POS terminal units if the configuration is deployed to multiple devices, verifying consistent correct messaging on all terminals.

Verify that after the configuration file correction, no other terminal messages related to gift card transactions have changed unexpectedly (e.g., approval message, decline message, balance inquiry message).
smoke_tests: With backend cloud processing disabled, cancel a single gift card transaction and confirm the POS terminal displays 'CANCEL TRANSACTION' — not 'VOID NEW ITEMS AND CANCEL TRANSACTION'.
Confirm the POS terminal successfully reaches the cancel message screen without freezing, erroring out, or displaying a blank screen when cloud processing is off.
Verify the POS terminal returns to a ready/idle state after displaying the 'CANCEL TRANSACTION' message.

coverage_depth.justification: Although this is a configuration value change (typically LOW risk), the scope is elevated to MEDIUM due to: multi-environment testing requirement (UAT, Pre-Production, Production), a potential second system requiring a corresponding change, ambiguity around retroactive vs. prospective application, multi-brand impact, and the financial reporting nature of the change where incorrect markup values directly affect revenue figures.

effort_estimate.notes: Lower bound assumes retroactive/prospective behaviour is clarified before testing begins and the third-party reporting platform change is confirmed as in-scope with a clear owner. clarification_flags: What specific file paths, directory paths, or process names does the script add as Windows Defender exclusions? This is critical to assess whether the exclusion scope is appropriately narrow or dangerously broad.
What is the exact version of the remote tunneling tool being excluded, and is there a version pinning mechanism to prevent the exclusion from silently applying to future versions of the tool?
What remote management or deployment platform is used to push the script to terminals (e.g., SCCM, Intune, proprietary RMM)? This affects integration test design and deployment targeting validation.
Which POS terminal hardware models and Windows OS versions are in scope? The spec mentions 'multiple lab environments' without specifying what variation exists between them.
Is the remote tunneling tool already installed on all targeted terminals, or does the script also handle installation? If installation is included, the functional scope expands considerably.
What is the rollback procedure if the exclusion causes unexpected behaviour? QA needs to know whether a tested rollback path exists and whether it should be validated.

Are there any PCI-DSS, internal security policy, or compliance requirements that govern antivirus exclusions on POS terminals? This may require sign-off testing or evidence capture beyond functional validation.
Has the script been reviewed or approved by a security team? If not, QA should flag that security review is a prerequisite before lab testing begins.
Does the exclusion need to be applied only once, or is it expected to be re-applied periodically (e.g., after Defender updates)? This affects idempotency and persistence test design.
What is the expected behaviour if the script is executed on a terminal that does not have the remote tunneling tool installed — should it still apply the exclusion, skip silently, or error?

coverage_depth.justification: This is an infrastructure and security configuration change rather than a new feature, but it carries meaningful risk: it modifies antivirus behaviour on production-adjacent POS terminals, involves a security tool exclusion that could widen attack surface, and must not disrupt live payment processing. MEDIUM depth is appropriate — thorough enough to catch security misconfigurations and POS regressions, but not requiring exhaustive combinatorial coverage.

effort_estimate.notes: Estimate assumes 2–3 lab terminal configurations (e.g., varying OS patch levels or hardware models). Lower bound reflects a single representative environment; upper bound accounts for multi-environment matrix testing, reboot persistence checks, and exploratory sessions. A small QA team of 1–2 testers should plan for 2–3 days of manual effort. Effort increases significantly if multiple POS terminal hardware variants or OS images must each be validated independently.

coverage_depth.justification: This is a payment processing firmware patch with direct impact on transaction integrity and financial data. The fix targets a specific failure mode (mid-transaction disconnect and reconnection failure) that must be validated across 6 device/POS combinations. The risk of regression in payment flows, potential for duplicate charges, and the safety-critical nature of payment terminals all justify high coverage depth.

Exploratory testing is time-boxed and not fully enumerable.

clarification_flags: Is the markup change prospective only (from the effective date forward) or does it apply retroactively to prior transactions? This fundamentally changes the regression and integration test scope.
What is the confirmed effective date, and is it a hard cutover at midnight or tied to a specific event (e.g., a pipeline run, a deployment window)? This affects boundary-date test case design.
Which specific third-party delivery platform is affected? Knowing the platform name and its integration method (API, SFTP, webhook, etc.) is required to design accurate integration tests.

Does the separate third-party reporting platform require a manual configuration change on their side, or is it driven automatically by the data feed from the internal system? This determines whether QA must coordinate with a vendor for testing.

Are both brands configured independently in the Data Mapping settings, or do they share a common configuration entry for this delivery platform? This affects the risk of one brand's change impacting the other.

What is the expected behaviour for transactions that span the effective date boundary (e.g., initiated before, settled after)? A business rule decision is needed before test cases can be written for this scenario.

Are there any downstream systems beyond the identified third-party reporting platform (e.g., finance/ERP exports, loyalty platforms, BI dashboards) that consume the delivery markup value and would need validation?
What does the data pipeline job schedule look like — is there a risk of in-flight pipeline runs during the configuration change that could apply mixed markup rates to the same batch?
Is there a rollback plan if the configuration change causes reporting discrepancies in Production, and should QA validate the rollback procedure as part of the test scope?

coverage_depth.justification: Although this is a configuration value change (typically LOW risk), the involvement of multiple environments (UAT, Pre-Prod, Production), two brands, a data pipeline, a separate third-party reporting platform, and an unresolved retroactivity question elevates the risk profile and integration surface area to MEDIUM. The effective date boundary and cross-platform reconciliation requirements add meaningful complexity beyond a simple config patch.

effort_estimate.notes: Lower bound assumes retroactivity is confirmed as out of scope and third-party reporting platform alignment is handled by the vendor. Upper bound applies if retroactive recalculation must be validated, time-zone boundary cases are in scope, and full reconciliation testing across all three environments is required. Estimates reflect manual execution by a small QA team and include re-execution across UAT, Pre-Production, and Production environments for smoke and key functional cases.

clarification_flags: How many distinct existing serialized coupon BIN ranges are currently configured in the CMS? This directly determines the volume of regression test cases required.
Is there a documented baseline or inventory of all existing BIN ranges and their expected behaviour (discount value, scope, limits) that QA can use as a reference for regression validation?
What is the exact numerical range of the new promotional BIN ranges? QA needs this to identify which existing BIN ranges are adjacent or potentially overlapping.
Does the CMS enforce uniqueness or non-overlap of BIN ranges at the configuration level, or is it possible for two records to claim the same BIN value without a system-level conflict warning?
Are there multiple POS terminal types or software versions in the UAT environment that each need to be tested, or is there a single standardised POS configuration?
Does the CMS content deployment to production use the same tooling and process as the UAT deployment? If not, the production promotion step itself is an untested risk.
What is the go-live date and the content deployment deadline? This affects how much time QA has and whether a phased or risk-prioritised approach is needed.
Are existing serialized coupons validated online (real-time CMS lookup) or offline (cached BIN table on POS)? This affects whether cache invalidation and sync behaviour must be tested.
Has the team that validated the new BIN ranges produced a test report or sign-off document? QA should confirm the scope of what was already tested to avoid duplication and identify gaps.
Are there any store-specific or region-specific BIN range configurations that differ from the default, which could be affected differently by the new additions?
Is coupon redemption state stored in the CMS, a separate redemption database, or on the POS itself? This affects the scope of integration and regression testing for single-use coupon enforcement.

coverage_depth.justification: This is a content record addition rather than a code change, which limits direct functional risk. However, BIN range configuration errors can silently misroute coupon lookups, corrupt redemption state, or affect financial reporting, warranting thorough boundary and regression coverage. The production deployment timeline adds urgency and reduces tolerance for missed defects.

effort_estimate.notes: Lower bound assumes a small set of existing serialized BIN ranges (5–10) with one representative test per range plus integration and smoke checks. Upper bound applies if there are 15+ existing BIN ranges requiring individual validation, multiple POS terminal types, or multiple store configurations in scope. Effort is manual and does not include automated regression. A pre-change BIN range baseline document would significantly reduce discovery time and tighten the estimate.

Attempt to scan a new promotional BIN coupon in a context where only existing serialized coupons should be valid (e.g., restricted tender type or restricted store) — confirm correct rejection behaviour

coverage_depth.justification: Certificate rotation is a high-risk, time-sensitive infrastructure change with a hard deadline tied to certificate expiry. A failure in production would cause complete loss of loyalty platform integration for the affected brand across all POS terminals and tablets. The change involves multiple device types, an external vendor dependency, and a content management configuration layer, all of which increase integration risk. Reversibility is limited once the old certificate expires, making pre-deployment validation critical.

effort_estimate.notes: Lower bound assumes a single POS terminal model and single tablet model are tested as representatives, the vendor certificate installation is confirmed before testing begins, and UAT environment zone closely mirrors production. Upper bound accounts for multiple device hardware variants, additional brand isolation verification, expanded error-path and timing scenarios, and any re-testing required if the vendor certificate installation is delayed or the UAT zone requires reconfiguration.

clarification_flags: Where exactly is the locked price stored — in the mobile app order payload, the order management database, or both — and which system is the authoritative source when the POS processes the order at fulfillment?

Does the POS re-query the pricing engine at fulfillment time, or does it consume the price values embedded in the order record? This is critical to understanding whether a price lock is architecturally enforced or assumed.

What is the payment model — is the customer charged in full at time of ordering, or is a hold placed and the final charge occurs at fulfillment? This affects which price-lock scenarios are financially relevant.
Is there any existing price-lock or order-snapshot mechanism documented in the system design, or is this behavior assumed/untested?
What admin interface or API is used to change item prices, and how quickly do price changes propagate to the systems involved (real-time, batch, cached)?
Are there any known environments or test data sets where advance orders and price changes can be safely simulated without affecting production data?
Does the scope include testing on both iOS and Android mobile app clients, and are there any known platform-specific differences in how orders are submitted?
Are promotions, coupons, or loyalty discounts applied at order time also expected to be locked, or only the base item price?
What constitutes a 'price change' in this system — only manual admin updates, or also automated pricing rules, surge pricing, or scheduled price changes?

coverage_depth.justification: This scenario has explicit product-decision urgency, involves financial data integrity (customers are charged real money at locked prices), spans multiple integrated systems (mobile app, pricing engine, order management, POS, payment processor), and the expected behavior has not been confirmed — meaning the outcome is unknown and regression risk is high. Thorough coverage is required to produce a reliable finding.

effort_estimate.notes: Lower bound assumes a single test environment with stable pricing engine access and direct POS inspection capability. Upper bound accounts for testing across multiple item types, price change magnitudes, and any additional edge cases surfaced during exploratory sessions. A small team of 2 QA practitioners should plan for 3–5 days including environment setup, test execution, and findings documentation given the cross-system nature of the flows.

Explore what happens if a price change is made and then reverted to the original price before fulfillment — does the system process correctly and are there any duplicate-charge or reconciliation anomalies?

Explore concurrent scenarios: simulate multiple advance orders for the same item being fulfilled simultaneously after a price change to check for race conditions or inconsistent price application.

coverage_depth.justification: This change directly affects POS configuration inheritance and menu page design delivery at the point of sale, which is a high-impact, customer-facing and revenue-critical system. Incorrect configuration could result in wrong menus being displayed, missing items, or limited-menu designs appearing at full-menu locations. The risk of regression to existing non-traditional and traditional zones is significant, and the configuration hierarchy is a shared infrastructure component. The change is a configuration addition but touches inheritance logic that could have broad downstream effects.

effort_estimate.notes: Lower bound assumes access to a staging or UAT environment with a pre-configured test property in the new zone and one in the existing limited-menu zone for direct comparison. Upper bound accounts for testing multiple properties in the new zone, additional regression coverage across more existing zone types, and exploratory scenarios requiring property reassignment. Effort increases significantly if physical or emulated POS terminals must be provisioned and synced manually for each scenario.

clarification_flags: The specification does not define which specific file paths, process names, or registry keys the script adds as exclusions — this is critical to verify the script's correctness and scope, and must be documented before testing begins
The exact version number of the remote tunneling tool being excluded is not stated — testers need this to confirm version-specificity of the exclusion and to test behaviour with other versions

The number and configuration of distinct lab environments to be tested is unspecified — the spec says 'multiple lab environments' but does not define how many or what differentiates them (OS build, Defender version, network config, etc.)
The deployment mechanism for the script is not defined (e.g., manual execution, SCCM, GPO, remote management platform push) — this affects integration test design and scope significantly
It is unclear whether any centralised antivirus management console or SIEM is in use that could override or alert on the exclusion — this affects both integration and exploratory test scope

The specification does not clarify whether terminals currently have the tunneling tool quarantined, not yet installed, or installed but blocked — each state may require a different pre-condition setup and test path

It is not stated whether any third-party EDR or endpoint security tooling is deployed alongside Windows Defender on these terminals, which could independently block the tool and fall outside the script's scope

The required user privilege level for script execution is not specified — testers need to know the intended execution context (SYSTEM, local admin, domain admin) to validate both success and failure paths
There is no rollback or remediation procedure defined in the spec — QA should clarify whether a rollback script exists and whether it also needs to be tested
It is unclear whether the exclusion is intended to be permanent or temporary, which affects regression testing around Defender definition updates and policy reapplication

coverage_depth.justification: This is an infrastructure/security configuration change (script deployment and AV exclusion) rather than a new feature or major version upgrade, but it carries meaningful risk: incorrect exclusion scope could weaken endpoint security, and misconfiguration could disrupt POS operations or remote support capability across multiple store locations. MEDIUM depth is appropriate — thorough functional and regression coverage is warranted, but full HIGH-depth coverage (e.g., extensive performance or load testing) is not justified.

effort_estimate.notes: Lower bound assumes a single representative lab environment and one OS/Defender version. Upper bound accounts for testing across multiple lab environment configurations, OS build variants, and network topologies as implied by the spec. Exploratory sessions should be timeboxed (suggest 3–4 sessions of 60–90 minutes each). A small QA team of 2 testers should plan for 3–5 days of effort including environment setup and evidence capture.

exploratory_tests: Probe whether the script behaves correctly on POS terminals running different Windows OS builds or Defender definition versions that may be present across store locations
Investigate behaviour when the script is executed while a Windows Defender scan is actively running on the terminal
Explore whether the exclusion script execution triggers any security alerts in a centralised SIEM or endpoint detection platform that could cause automated remediation to reverse the exclusion
Test script execution on a terminal where the remote tunneling tool binary is currently running (active process) to check for file-lock conflicts or partial exclusion application
Investigate whether the exclusion path is case-sensitive or uses environment variables that may resolve differently across terminal configurations (e.g., non-standard Windows installation drives)
Probe the behaviour if the script is executed by a user account with insufficient privileges — verify it fails gracefully with a clear error rather than silently partially applying
Explore whether a Windows Defender definition update pushed shortly after script execution could re-flag the tool before the exclusion is re-evaluated
Investigate whether any third-party security tooling deployed alongside Defender (e.g., EDR agents) independently flags the tunneling tool and would not be addressed by this script
functional_tests: Execute the antivirus exclusion script on a lab POS terminal and verify that the target remote tunneling tool's file path(s) are present in Windows Defender exclusion list post-execution
Execute the script and confirm the remote tunneling tool can establish a remote support session without being quarantined or blocked by Windows Defender
Verify that the exclusion script completes without error codes or failure messages across each distinct lab environment configuration
Confirm that the exclusion applies only to the specified version of the remote tunneling tool and not to older or newer versions not listed in the script
Verify that the script does not add exclusions beyond those explicitly defined in the specification (no over-broad directory or wildcard exclusions unintentionally included)
Run the script on a terminal where the tool has already been quarantined and verify the quarantine is cleared and the tool becomes operational
Verify that re-running the script on a terminal where the exclusion already exists does not cause duplicate entries, errors, or system instability
Confirm that the exclusion persists after a Windows Defender definition update is applied following script execution
Verify the exclusion persists after a POS terminal reboot
integration_tests: Validate that the remote tunneling tool, once excluded, can successfully establish a full remote support session from a support technician's workstation to the POS terminal end-to-end
Verify that during an active remote support session (via the now-excluded tool), POS transactions can still be processed without interruption or data corruption

Confirm that the script deployment mechanism (e.g., remote management platform, GPO, SCCM, or manual push) successfully delivers and executes the script on terminals across different store network configurations
Verify that any centralised antivirus management console (if in use) correctly reflects the exclusion state of the terminal after script execution
Validate that the POS terminal's payment integration (card processing/PIN pad) remains fully operational after the exclusion script is applied and a remote session is active simultaneously
regression_tests: Verify that existing Windows Defender exclusions on the terminal (if any were previously configured) are preserved and not removed or overwritten by the script
Confirm that other known-malicious file detections are still caught by Windows Defender after the exclusion is applied (AV is not globally weakened)
Verify that POS end-of-day reporting and reconciliation functions complete correctly on a terminal where the script has been applied
Confirm that scheduled Windows Defender scans still execute on their configured schedule after the exclusion is applied
Verify that the POS terminal's connection to the back-office or head-office system (e.g., price updates, inventory sync) is unaffected after script execution
Confirm that receipt printing, cash drawer, and peripheral device integrations function normally post-script execution
Verify that any existing remote management or monitoring agents on the terminal continue to operate normally alongside the newly excluded tool
Confirm that Windows Defender threat history and reporting are intact and accessible after the script runs
smoke_tests: After script execution, launch the POS application and confirm it starts successfully and reaches the ready-to-transact state
Process a basic end-to-end sale transaction (cash and card) on a POS terminal where the script has been applied and verify no errors occur
Confirm Windows Defender real-time protection remains enabled after the script is applied (i.e., the script does not disable AV protection globally)
Verify the remote management tool can connect to the terminal from a support workstation within 2 minutes of script execution
Confirm no unexpected Windows Event Log errors or warnings are generated immediately following script execution

clarification_flags: What is the exact network topology — is the terminal connected directly to the POS via a local cable, or through a network switch/router? This affects how 'cable unplug' is simulated and whether the fix applies equally to all physical configurations.

Does the fix apply to all three terminal models (A, B, C) via the same firmware binary, or are there model-specific firmware variants? If model-specific, are all three confirmed to have updated firmware available from the vendor?
Is there a specific quick chip protocol version or EMV kernel version referenced in the vendor fix notes? This would help scope which card types and entry modes are most at risk.

What is the expected reconnection behaviour by design — should the terminal auto-reconnect without any operator action, or is a specific operator step (e.g. pressing a key) required? This is needed to define pass/fail criteria.
Are there any known differences in how POS v18 and v19 handle terminal communication errors or timeouts that could affect how the reconnection fix manifests on each version?

Is there a payment processor/acquirer test environment available for integration testing, or will testing be performed against a live environment with test cards? This affects risk and test data management.
What is the rollback plan if the new firmware introduces regressions — is remote firmware rollback supported, and has it been tested by the vendor?
Are there any other concurrent changes being deployed alongside this firmware update (e.g. POS software patches, network configuration changes) that could confound test results?
Does the fix address only Ethernet/wired disconnection, or does it also cover Wi-Fi or other network interface types if any terminal models support them?

coverage_depth.justification: Although this is a vendor patch fix (suggesting LOW), the change touches the payment processing integration layer which is high-risk for financial and data integrity issues. The requirement to test across 6 device/POS version combinations significantly increases surface area. MEDIUM depth is appropriate to validate the specific fix, protect adjacent payment flows, and ensure no regressions across the matrix without over-investing in exhaustive scenario coverage.

effort_estimate.notes: Base test cases (functional, smoke, regression, integration, exploratory) number approximately 25–30 scenarios, but each must be executed across 6 device/POS combinations for the core disconnect/reconnect and smoke flows, multiplying effort materially. Some regression and integration tests can be sampled across a representative subset (e.g. 2–3 combinations) rather than all 6. Estimate assumes a small QA team executing manually; allow 2–3 days for full matrix execution including setup and device firmware flashing time.

exploratory_tests: Unplug and reconnect the network cable repeatedly in rapid succession (3–5 times) before attempting a new transaction, and observe whether the terminal stabilises and reconnects reliably or enters a fault state

Attempt a transaction immediately during the reconnection window (before the terminal has fully re-established the connection) and observe whether the POS presents a clear 'not ready' message or allows a transaction attempt that then fails

Investigate behaviour when the network cable is disconnected during the PIN entry or signature step specifically, rather than earlier in the quick chip flow, to determine if the fix scope covers all transaction stages
Check terminal behaviour if the network is restored but the POS application has timed out or moved to a different screen — does the terminal recover cleanly or require operator action
Probe whether the fix introduces any change in transaction speed or quick chip timing under normal (no disconnect) conditions that could affect customer experience

Test firmware update rollback: if the new firmware is reverted to the previous version, does the original reconnection bug reappear as expected, confirming the fix is firmware-specific and not environmental
functional_tests: Unplug network cable from payment terminal mid-transaction (after card tap/insert but before authorisation response) and confirm transaction fails gracefully with a user-facing communication error message rather than hanging or crashing

After mid-transaction cable disconnect and failure, reconnect network cable and immediately attempt a new card-present transaction — confirm the terminal successfully re-establishes connection and the transaction completes without manual intervention or device restart

Verify that the quick chip match sequence completes correctly under normal conditions (no disconnect) on each of the 6 device/POS version combinations (POS v18 + Terminal A, B, C; POS v19 + Terminal A, B, C)
Simulate cable reconnection after varying delay intervals (immediate, 10 seconds, 30 seconds, 2 minutes) and confirm successful reconnection and transaction completion in each case
Confirm that the failed mid-disconnect transaction is correctly voided or rolled back and does not result in a partial charge or dangling authorisation on the payment processor side
Verify that after reconnection, the terminal correctly identifies and processes quick chip (EMV contactless) transactions, not falling back to an incorrect card read mode
Confirm that the firmware version reported by the terminal management interface matches the expected new firmware version string on all three terminal models
integration_tests: Confirm that authorisation requests and responses are correctly transmitted to and received from the payment processor/acquirer host after firmware update, with no message format or protocol version regressions

Verify that transaction records written to the POS back-office or reporting database are complete and accurate for transactions that experienced a mid-transaction disconnect followed by a successful retry

Confirm that the failed disconnect transaction does not appear as a settled or authorised record in the payment processor portal, and that any held authorisation is released within the expected timeframe

If a terminal management system (TMS) is used for firmware deployment, verify that the firmware update is correctly recorded in the TMS audit log and device inventory reflects the new firmware version
Validate that any loyalty, discount, or surcharge integrations triggered during the payment flow are not disrupted by the firmware change on either POS version
regression_tests: Process a full sale, then perform a same-session void/refund and confirm the reversal flow completes correctly on all 6 combinations
Complete a split-tender transaction (e.g. partial card, partial cash) and confirm amounts are correctly allocated and receipts are accurate
Verify end-of-day settlement/batch close completes successfully and totals reconcile with transaction log after transactions that included a mid-session disconnect event
Confirm that a transaction declined by the payment processor (e.g. insufficient funds) is handled correctly and the terminal returns to ready state without requiring a restart
Verify that signature capture or PIN entry prompts (where applicable per terminal model) still behave correctly post-firmware update
Confirm that receipt printing (where integrated) is not disrupted and receipt data accurately reflects transaction outcome
Verify that the POS transaction history and reporting screens correctly reflect completed, failed, and voided transactions including those affected by the disconnect scenario
Test that a second consecutive mid-transaction disconnect (i.e. disconnect, reconnect, transact, disconnect again) still results in graceful failure and successful subsequent reconnection
smoke_tests: On each of the 6 device/POS version combinations, complete a standard card-present (chip) transaction end-to-end with no network interruption to confirm baseline payment flow is intact post-firmware update
On each combination, complete a contactless/quick chip transaction end-to-end with no network interruption
Confirm the POS application successfully detects and communicates with the payment terminal on startup after firmware update, with no pairing or handshake errors
Process a manual card entry (keyed) transaction on at least one terminal per POS version to confirm non-chip flows are unaffected
